paragraphs: Linear contextual bandit algorithms make decisions while learning how observed features relate to rewards. Many approaches rely on estimating the parameters of a linear model. A familiar theoretical argument establishes that sufficiently accurate estimates can produce low regret, meaning a small cumulative shortfall relative to better decisions. This paper investigates the reverse relationship: what does successful decision-making imply about estimation?

The authors construct a general transformation that turns a linear contextual bandit algorithm into an estimator for a linear model. They show that the resulting estimator’s error is controlled by the algorithm’s regret. Consequently, a low-regret algorithm must yield an accurate estimator through this transformation, even if parameter estimation is not the algorithm’s explicit organizing principle.

This relationship provides a route to proving limits on bandit performance. Estimation lower bounds can help establish regret lower bounds, connecting the analysis of sequential decisions to linear regression. The contribution therefore complements existing sufficiency arguments with a necessity result and a reusable analytical reduction.
icml-2022-a-reduction-from-linear-contex.tldr: A general reduction shows that low-regret linear contextual bandit algorithms must induce accurate linear-model estimators.

paragraphs: Adversarial training seeks to protect models against inputs deliberately altered to cause mistakes. This paper examines that problem when classes are highly uneven: common classes have many examples, while rare classes have few. The authors focus on AUC because its insensitivity to class distribution makes it a more appropriate objective than accuracy for their long-tail setting.

Directly optimizing adversarial AUC creates a computational obstacle. Positive and negative examples are coupled in the objective, so generating adversarial examples would require scanning the complete dataset. AdAUC uses concavity regularization to reformulate the objective as a saddle point problem whose terms operate on individual examples. This reformulation enables an end-to-end training procedure.

The paper also establishes a convergence guarantee for the proposed algorithm. Its analysis addresses the extra complication of producing adversarial examples through gradients of a min-max problem. Experiments on three long-tail datasets provide evidence for the method’s performance and robustness, supporting adversarial AUC optimization as a practical direction for imbalanced learning.
icml-2022-adauc-end-to-end-adversarial-a.tldr: AdAUC reformulates adversarial AUC optimization to enable end-to-end robust training on datasets with highly imbalanced classes.

paragraphs: Conditional generators aim to produce data with a requested label while preserving the variation found within each class. The paper investigates why auxiliary classifier GANs can generate too little of that variation. Its explanation centers on a classifier that is unaware of the generator: the guidance it supplies can reduce conditional entropy instead of helping match the joint distribution of data and labels.

ADC-GAN changes the auxiliary classifier so that it distinguishes class labels for real and generated examples. This makes the classifier generator-aware and changes the information available to guide generation. The intervention targets the source of the diversity problem identified by the authors rather than simply adding another preference for varied outputs.

The theoretical analysis shows that the generator can learn the joint distribution even without the original discriminator. The authors connect this property to stable training and robustness to the weighting coefficient and GAN loss choice. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report superior conditional generation relative to the classifier-based and projection-based methods considered.
icml-2022-conditional-gans-with-auxiliar.tldr: ADC-GAN uses a generator-aware auxiliary classifier to address reduced within-class diversity in conditional GANs.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains a shared model using data held by multiple clients, with communication between those clients and a server. Repeatedly exchanging model parameters can create a substantial communication burden. Quantization addresses this by representing parameters with fewer possible values, allowing the information sent during training to be compressed.

DAdaQuant makes the quantization level adaptive along two dimensions: it changes over the course of training and differs across clients. The central idea is that a single fixed compression setting need not be the best choice for every participant or every stage. The authors find that dynamically adjusting this setting can improve compression while preserving model quality.

In the reported experiments, DAdaQuant consistently improves compression for messages traveling from clients to the server. Its gains reach up to 2.8 times those of the strongest non-adaptive baselines. This result concerns the communication direction evaluated, and shows the practical value of treating quantization as a changing training decision rather than a fixed configuration.
icml-2022-dadaquant-doubly-adaptive-quan.tldr: DAdaQuant adapts quantization across clients and training time, improving client-to-server compression by up to 2.8 times over non-adaptive baselines.

paragraphs: In a bandit problem, a learner chooses actions and uses their rewards to improve future choices. Rewards from different actions may be related, as with preferences for products belonging to common categories. This paper models those relationships through a hierarchical Bayesian structure with hidden variables. Multiple layers allow the hierarchy to describe more complex patterns of dependence.

The proposed algorithm, hierarchical Thompson sampling or HierTS, uses this structure when choosing actions. For Gaussian hierarchies, the authors derive an exact hierarchical representation of the posterior distribution. That representation makes efficient implementation possible and provides the basis for analyzing the algorithm’s Bayes regret, a measure of decision-making loss averaged under the Bayesian model.

The resulting bounds reflect the problem’s structure: more informative priors reduce the regret bounds, and the expressions can highlight reduced dependence on the number of actions. Synthetic and real-world experiments support these theoretical findings. The work demonstrates how explicitly representing relationships among actions can improve the statistical efficiency of learning.
icml-2022-deep-hierarchy-in-bandits-ddee.tldr: HierTS exploits multilayer Bayesian relationships among action rewards, with efficient Gaussian inference and regret bounds that reflect those relationships.

paragraphs: Generating a molecule in three dimensions requires describing both which atoms are present and where they are located. This paper introduces EDM, a diffusion model that handles those two kinds of information together. Atom positions are continuous quantities, while atom identities are categorical, so the model’s denoising network jointly operates on different types of features.

The network is equivariant to Euclidean transformations. In practical terms, changing the spatial placement or orientation of a molecular configuration produces a corresponding transformation in the model’s spatial behavior. This builds geometric consistency into the generation process. The approach learns to remove the noise introduced by a diffusion process while respecting that structure.

The authors also provide a probabilistic analysis that permits likelihood computation for molecules under the model. Their experiments report significantly better generated-sample quality and training efficiency than previous three-dimensional molecular generation methods. The contribution combines joint modeling of atom types and coordinates, geometric symmetry, and a probabilistic treatment that supports both generation and likelihood evaluation.
icml-2022-equivariant-diffusion-for-mole.tldr: EDM jointly denoises atom types and coordinates with geometric equivariance, improving molecular sample quality and training efficiency in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Self-supervised encoders need to learn representations that distinguish inputs. Complete feature collapse defeats that purpose by mapping every input to the same vector. Whitening has been proposed as an explicit way to prevent collapse. This paper studies the space between those extremes, using power-law decay in feature eigenvalues and an exponent, beta, to describe that spectrum.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical evidence that choices such as projection layers and regularization strength influence the eigenvalue decay rate. They also show that the degree of whitening affects generalization, especially when few labels are available. This shifts attention from merely avoiding a constant representation to understanding how information is distributed across representation directions.

Those findings motivate PostMan-Pat, a method that efficiently post-processes a pretrained encoder to enforce a chosen power-law decay rate. Across a range of self-supervised methods and encoder architectures, the authors report improved label efficiency and transferability. The results suggest that adjusting a learned representation’s spectrum can improve its usefulness after pretraining.
icml-2022-exploring-the-gap-between-coll.tldr: PostMan-Pat adjusts pretrained feature spectra, improving label efficiency and transferability across the tested self-supervised encoders.

paragraphs: Some generative models learn a mapping from a familiar distribution, such as a Gaussian, to the unknown distribution represented by observed data. Finding that mapping can involve searching through a large class of nonlinear functions implemented by neural networks. Although effective, this process can demand increasing runtime and memory as applications require better performance.

The paper proposes a simpler and substantially cheaper strategy based on forward operator estimation. It adapts existing results about kernel transfer operators to the generative modeling problem. The resulting formulation supports both approximating a data distribution and drawing samples from it, making the operator approach useful for the central tasks expected of a generative model.

The authors report favorable empirical comparisons with powerful baselines alongside substantial runtime savings. They also demonstrate good performance with small samples in a brain-imaging setting. These findings make computational efficiency a central part of the contribution: the proposed formulation offers a different way to obtain useful distribution approximations and samples with lower reported computational cost.
icml-2022-forward-operator-estimation-in.tldr: Kernel transfer operators provide a simpler generative modeling approach with favorable empirical performance and substantial runtime savings.

paragraphs: The path taken by a stochastic optimizer may matter for how well a trained model performs beyond its training data. Earlier work connected generalization to heavy-tailed optimization behavior, largely through continuous-time approximations. This paper develops a treatment that also covers the discrete updates used by the original optimization algorithms.

The analysis first bounds generalization using a mathematical quantity called the Fernique-Talagrand functional applied to the optimizer’s trajectory. This makes the bound depend on both the data and the algorithm. The authors then use the optimizer’s Markov structure to express bounds through its transition kernel, which describes how one optimization state leads probabilistically to another.

The resulting bounds connect generalization with the transition kernel’s lower tail exponent around a local minimum, in both discrete and continuous time. Experiments across several neural networks show correlations between these exponents and generalization error. Those correlations support the theoretical direction without establishing that the exponent alone determines performance. The contribution provides a more direct mathematical connection between optimization dynamics and generalization.
icml-2022-generalization-bounds-using-lo.tldr: New bounds connect generalization to stochastic optimizer transition kernels and their lower tail exponents, including for discrete-time updates.

paragraphs: Pairwise comparisons describe how two items relate, but many applications need a single ranking of all items. GNNRank approaches this problem by representing comparisons as a directed graph. Competitors or other ranked entities become nodes, and their comparisons become directed edges. This representation lets a neural network learn from the pattern of comparisons across the graph.

The framework combines directed-graph embeddings with ranking-score estimation and new objectives that capture ranking upsets or violations. It also incorporates a specific structural preference by unfolding the computation of a Fiedler vector for a graph built from a learnable similarity matrix. This places a graph-based ranking computation inside the trainable approach.

Experiments across extensive datasets show performance that is competitive with, and often better than, the evaluated baselines. The authors also report promising transfer ability. Together, these findings support learning a graph representation for ranking recovery, while retaining an explicit connection to the structure of ranking disagreements and to a graph-derived ordering mechanism.
icml-2022-gnnrank-learning-global-rankin.tldr: GNNRank learns global rankings from directed comparison graphs using ranking-aware objectives and a graph-structured scoring approach.

paragraphs: A Transformer serving several tasks needs a way to adapt its behavior to each task while sharing useful information across them. HyperPrompt addresses this through learned prompts that condition self-attention. A separate HyperNetwork generates these hyper-prompts, and the entire system learns them end to end rather than relying on manually written instructions.

The generated prompts act as task-level memories that attention queries can consult. This allows the model to learn task-specific feature maps while retaining flexible information sharing between tasks. The design therefore places task conditioning within the attention mechanism, with a small additional parameter budget devoted to expressing differences among tasks.

The authors report competitive results against strong multitask baselines with as little as 0.14% additional task-conditioning parameters. Across many model sizes on GLUE and SuperGLUE, experiments show that HyperPrompt can outperform T5 multitask baselines and parameter-efficient alternatives including Prompt-Tuning and HyperFormer++. These results support its combination of parameter efficiency, computational efficiency, and effective task adaptation in the evaluated language-understanding settings.
icml-2022-hyperprompt-prompt-based-task-.tldr: HyperPrompt generates task-specific attention prompts with a HyperNetwork, enabling efficient multitask adaptation and strong language-understanding results.

paragraphs: Knowing a classifier’s overall performance does not explain whether its errors follow recognizable patterns. This paper seeks interpretable combinations of feature values that strongly correlate with correct or incorrect predictions. The aim is a global description of a classifier’s behavior that can reveal systematic weaknesses and suggest where improvement efforts should focus.

The authors cast this task as a broader label-description problem and formulate it using the Minimum Description Length principle. They develop Premise, an efficient algorithm for finding a useful set of descriptive patterns. Because the patterns describe relationships between features and prediction outcomes, the approach can be applied to arbitrary classifiers.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show strong practical performance, including recovery of ground-truth patterns in highly imbalanced data with many features. Case studies in Visual Question Answering and Named Entity Recognition show clear, actionable descriptions of systematic errors. The result is a way to turn collections of mistakes into interpretable regularities, while keeping the stated relationship correlational.
icml-2022-label-descriptive-patterns-and.tldr: Premise discovers interpretable feature patterns associated with classifier successes and errors, helping characterize systematic weaknesses.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether knowledge acquired by language models can support action in interactive environments. The task is to turn a high-level natural-language request into a sequence of more concrete steps. The authors find that sufficiently large pretrained models, when prompted appropriately, can produce useful mid-level plans without additional training.

A practical obstacle remains: a plausible verbal instruction may not correspond precisely to an action the environment accepts. The proposed procedure conditions on existing demonstrations and translates plans semantically into admissible actions. Thus, the planning result does not require further model training, but the action-grounding procedure does use demonstrations to help connect language to the environment.

In VirtualHome, the method substantially improves executability relative to the language-model baseline. Human evaluation also identifies a trade-off between executable plans and correct plans: making steps acceptable to the environment does not by itself ensure that they accomplish the intended task. The findings offer qualified evidence that language models contain knowledge that can be extracted for actionable planning.
icml-2022-language-models-as-zero-shot-p.tldr: Large language models can produce plans without further training, while demonstration-conditioned action translation improves executability with a correctness trade-off.

paragraphs: Inverse folding asks which protein sequence fits a given arrangement of backbone atoms. Learning this relationship has been constrained by the number of experimentally determined protein structures. This paper expands the available training material by using AlphaFold2 to predict structures for 12 million sequences, increasing the training data by nearly three orders of magnitude.

The model is a sequence-to-sequence Transformer with invariant geometric layers for processing the structural input. Trained with the additional predicted structures, it achieves 51% native sequence recovery on structurally held-out backbones and 72% recovery for buried residues. The overall recovery result improves on existing methods by almost 10 percentage points.

The authors also report generalization to more complex settings, including protein complexes, partially masked structures, binding interfaces, and multiple states. These findings show the usefulness of predicted structures as training data for learning the structure-to-sequence relationship. The reported recovery figures describe agreement with native sequences, while the additional tasks demonstrate the breadth of structural inputs and design settings the model can handle.
icml-2022-learning-inverse-folding-from-.tldr: Training on millions of predicted protein structures improves inverse folding, reaching 51% native sequence recovery on structurally held-out backbones.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning under a specific structural assumption: rewards and transition probabilities are linear in a feature representation of states and actions. The setting consists of finite episodes whose dynamics may vary across steps. Within this linear Markov decision process framework, the objective is efficient learning with regret close to the best achievable worst-case rate.

The proposed algorithm, LSVI-UCB+, combines weighted ridge regression with upper-confidence value iteration and a Bernstein-type exploration bonus. These components support learning value estimates while accounting for uncertainty during exploration. The proof introduces a new Bernstein self-normalized bound and a refined treatment of a correction term needed for the statistical analysis.

The resulting regret bound scales as H times d times the square root of T, up to logarithmic factors, where H is episode length, d is feature dimension, and T counts steps. It matches the stated lower bound to that precision, closing a square-root-of-Hd gap in prior upper bounds. The near-optimality claim applies to the specified linear MDP setting.
icml-2022-nearly-minimax-optimal-reinfor.tldr: LSVI-UCB+ achieves computationally efficient learning with regret matching the linear-MDP minimax lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Neural differential-equation models learn how a system evolves, but ordinary differential equations are inadequate for the long-range dependencies and discontinuities highlighted in this paper. Neural ODE approaches also encounter numerical instability with stiff dynamics and piecewise forcing. Neural Laplace seeks a unified framework for these cases and for broader equation classes involving delays or accumulated history.

The method learns in the Laplace domain rather than directly describing changes over time. In that representation, history dependence and time-domain discontinuities can be expressed through sums of complex exponentials. The authors also use a stereographic mapping associated with the Riemann sphere to encourage greater smoothness in the Laplace representation and make learning more efficient.

Experiments show superior modeling and extrapolation of trajectories across diverse differential-equation classes, including systems with complicated history dependence and abrupt changes. The contribution is a shared representation for learning several kinds of dynamics. Its reported results cover both fitting trajectories and extending predictions beyond the observed portion of those trajectories.
icml-2022-neural-laplace-learning-divers.tldr: Neural Laplace learns dynamics in the Laplace domain to model diverse differential equations, including systems with memory and abrupt changes.

paragraphs: This paper studies approximate logical relationships among neurons inside a neural network. Its Neuron Dependency Graph represents each neuron through a Boolean activation value and draws a directed edge when one activation approximately implies another. The graph turns internal activity into a symbolic description of dependencies that can be inspected at the level of individual neurons.

The authors find that dependencies extracted using training data generalize well to test data. This matters because a description of internal structure is more useful when its relationships extend beyond the examples used to discover them. The resulting graph provides an interpretable account of how activation patterns relate within the network.

The paper also connects these graphs to Structural Causal Models. Empirical tests show that an NDG can behave as a causal abstraction of its corresponding neural network, responding consistently with that network under interventions in the framework used by the authors. The claim is supported empirically, and the graph’s logical implications remain approximate rather than exact universal rules.
icml-2022-neuron-dependency-graphs-a-cau.tldr: Neuron Dependency Graphs summarize approximate logical activation relationships and empirically support a causal abstraction of neural networks.

paragraphs: A regression network’s prediction does not by itself indicate how uncertain the model is. This paper studies that uncertainty with scarce, noiseless training data, isolating uncertainty about the model from observation noise. The authors identify five desired properties and find that established benchmark methods do not reliably capture some of them, including properties required by Bayesian theory.

NOMU uses two connected neural subnetworks: one predicts the target, and the other represents model uncertainty. A specially designed training loss works with this architecture to enforce the five proposed properties. Its modular structure also allows it to supply uncertainty for an already trained network, provided the original training data are available.

The evaluations cover regression and noiseless Bayesian optimization with expensive evaluations. NOMU performs at least as well as the state-of-the-art methods considered for regression and outperforms all considered benchmarks in Bayesian optimization. These results support the architecture’s usefulness in the studied scarce-data, noiseless setting, where uncertainty estimates can guide decisions about costly evaluations.
icml-2022-nomu-neural-optimization-based.tldr: NOMU couples prediction and uncertainty subnetworks to enforce five uncertainty properties and performs strongly in scarce-data, noiseless evaluations.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning develops a policy from previously collected data, without gathering new experience through exploration. This paper examines the discount factor, which controls how future rewards enter the learning objective. Although its effects have been studied in online learning, the authors investigate what it does when learning must rely on a fixed dataset.

Their theoretical analysis identifies two roles. First, the discount factor acts as a regulator that trades optimality against sample efficiency when used with existing offline methods. Second, a lower guidance discount factor can express pessimism: the resulting policy optimization can be understood in terms of performance under the worst possible models.

Experiments with tabular decision processes and standard D4RL tasks support these theoretical observations. The reported effects appear both with small datasets alongside existing offline techniques and with larger datasets without other conservative methods. The findings make the discount factor a consequential design choice for offline learning, with distinct regularization and pessimism interpretations rather than a guarantee that lowering it always helps.
icml-2022-on-the-role-of-discount-factor.tldr: The discount factor shapes offline reinforcement learning through both an optimality–sample-efficiency trade-off and a pessimistic optimization effect.

paragraphs: Agents cooperating on a task may behave differently because they have different attributes or goals. This paper proposes role diversity as a way to quantify those differences and connect them to policy performance. The measure considers three perspectives: agents’ actions, their trajectories through a task, and their contributions to the collective outcome.

The theoretical analysis decomposes a multi-agent learning error bound into three parts that are strongly related to role diversity. These factors bear on three common policy-design choices: sharing parameters among agents, providing communication mechanisms, and assigning credit for outcomes. The framework therefore connects measurable behavioral differences with decisions about how a cooperative learning system should be organized.

Experiments in the Multiagent Particle Environment and the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge support role diversity as a robust description of cooperation tasks. The authors show that it can help diagnose whether a policy fits the current multi-agent system. Its value lies in explaining task–policy fit and informing policy optimization through several complementary views of agent differences.
icml-2022-policy-diagnosis-via-measuring.tldr: Role diversity measures differences in agents’ actions, trajectories, and contributions to help diagnose cooperative multi-agent policies.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection aims to recognize examples outside the kinds of data a model is expected to handle. This paper moves evaluation beyond small, simple settings toward high-resolution images, thousands of classes, multiple labels, and spatial anomaly detection. Its central contribution includes benchmarks that make these larger and more varied settings accessible for further study.

For ImageNet multiclass detectors, the authors introduce Species, containing more than 700,000 images and over a thousand anomalous species. They use ImageNet-21K to evaluate multilabel detectors associated with PASCAL VOC and COCO. A third benchmark evaluates anomaly segmentation using road anomalies, extending the problem from recognizing unusual images to identifying anomalous regions.

Across the reported large-scale multiclass, multilabel, and segmentation tasks, a simple detector based on the maximum logit outperforms prior methods. A logit is a model score before conversion into a probability. The result establishes a straightforward baseline across the new evaluations and shows why methods should be tested under broader conditions before judging their relative effectiveness.
icml-2022-scaling-out-of-distribution-de.tldr: New large-scale anomaly benchmarks reveal that a simple maximum-logit detector outperforms prior methods across the evaluated task types.

paragraphs: Network pruning removes parameters and is often expected to reduce both computation and overfitting. This paper reports that pruning can sometimes make overfitting worse. Across extensive experiments, increasing sparsity produces a non-monotonic pattern: test performance first deteriorates, then improves, and finally deteriorates again. The authors call this phenomenon sparse double descent.

Their interpretation attributes the initial decline to greater overfitting, the recovery to reduced overfitting, and the final decline to loss of useful information. To help explain the pattern, they examine the l2 distance between a sparse model’s initialized and final parameters. They propose that this learning distance may track the sparse double-descent curve well and reflect generalization better than minima flatness.

The findings also qualify expectations around the lottery ticket hypothesis: a subnetwork regarded as a winning ticket may not always win in this setting. The practical implication is that removing more parameters does not necessarily improve generalization smoothly. Sparsity itself can create a changing balance between overfitting and retained information.
icml-2022-sparse-double-descent-where-ne.tldr: Pruning can worsen, relieve, and then worsen test performance as sparsity increases, a phenomenon termed sparse double descent.

paragraphs: This paper revisits Transformer components to improve their handling of long sequences while preserving language-modeling quality. The first change is a gated attention unit, a simple layer that permits a weaker single-head attention mechanism with only a small quality loss. This establishes a different building block for constructing an efficient sequence model.

The authors then introduce a complementary linear approximation designed to work efficiently on accelerators. Combining it with the gated attention unit produces FLASH. The two changes are linked: the new layer makes simpler attention viable, and the approximation provides an efficient way to use that design while remaining competitive in quality.

FLASH matches the perplexity of improved Transformers at context lengths of both 512 and 8K. Reported training speedups reach 4.9 times on Wiki-40B and 12.1 times on PG-19 for autoregressive modeling, and 4.8 times on C4 for masked modeling. These are task-specific reported maxima, with perplexity matching providing the stated evidence that faster training preserves language-modeling quality in those evaluations.
icml-2022-transformer-quality-in-linear-.tldr: FLASH combines gated attention with a linear approximation to match improved Transformer perplexity while substantially accelerating training.

paragraphs: Contextualized embeddings represent language in ways that depend on its surrounding text. This paper proposes a fully unsupervised method for detecting bias within those representations. Its source of information is the structure of social networks, specifically the assortative patterns they implicitly encode. The method seeks an embedding subspace that captures information associated with those patterns.

The approach combines graph neural networks, orthogonality regularization, and structured sparsity learning. Together, these components support identifying the relevant portion of the embedding space. The authors develop ideological bias as a concrete application, introduce an ideological subspace, and show how to recover and probe it using online discussion forums.

The experiments suggest that this subspace contains abstract evaluative semantics and reflects changes in the political left–right spectrum during Donald Trump’s presidency. These are qualified empirical interpretations of the recovered representation. The contribution is a way to investigate socially associated information inside contextualized embeddings without supervised bias labels, using network structure to guide the discovery.
icml-2022-unsupervised-detection-of-cont.tldr: An unsupervised method uses social-network structure to identify embedding subspaces associated with bias, demonstrated through ideological information in discussion forums.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks represent uncertainty through distributions over their weights, but sampling from the posterior can be difficult. This paper introduces repriorisation, a data-dependent change of parameter coordinates. In the transformed representation, the posterior’s KL divergence from the network prior tends to zero as layer widths grow, giving a simple description of the wide-network limit in parameter space.

This result complements the known Gaussian-process description of wide networks in function space. The authors use the parameter transformation to develop a Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling algorithm. Its mixing improves as the network becomes wider, an unusual outcome given the difficulties MCMC commonly faces as dimensionality increases.

Experiments with fully connected and residual networks show up to 50 times higher effective sample size than sampling without reparameterization. Improvements occur at every width tested, and the advantage grows with layer width. The asymptotic theoretical result and the finite-network experiments jointly support changing parameter coordinates as a practical route to more effective Bayesian posterior sampling.
icml-2022-wide-bayesian-neural-networks-.tldr: Repriorisation simplifies wide Bayesian neural-network posteriors in transformed coordinates and accelerates MCMC sampling, with gains increasing with width.
